case_study_insert.main_stem: Tarrant Rubber Mouldings (TRM) is a partnership in the rubber-products sector, employing a workforce of 38. Founded in 2013 by Dev Tarrant, it makes moulded rubber seals and gaskets for car manufacturers and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. TRM plans to invest $480,000 in a new injection-moulding machine with a recycled-rubber feed system, financed by a $180,000 bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $175,000 a year, a variable cost of $9.00 a unit and a selling price of $16.00, and currently produces 45,000 units a year. TRM faces two problems: labour turnover has reached 14% and waste from rubber off-cuts on the line is rising steadily.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — Q2 2025: The moulding line produced 11,250 gaskets last quarter at a defect rate of 3.6%, up from 2.4% a year ago, with off-cut waste costing $16 per kilogram. Customer complaints rose from 14 to 27 per month. Average delivery lead time is 7 days. A survey of 200 automotive buyers found that 71% prefer suppliers using recycled rubber, and 48% check environmental credentials before ordering. A skills audit shows 12 of 38 staff lack injection-moulding certification; on-the-job training is available internally, while off-the-job courses at the local college cost $780 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Tarrant Rubber Mouldings as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 3.75% to 4.50%, raising borrowing costs for smaller firms. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.1% from $13.50 to $14.46 per hour from April 2026. (3) Synthetic and natural rubber input costs have risen 8.7% year-on-year, inflation is 5.9%, and car production grew 3.2%.

questions.question_text: TRM is financing its $480,000 moulding machine with a $180,000 bank loan and $300,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for TRM of using the bank loan rather than relying only on retained profit.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: The $180,000 bank loan lets TRM keep the $300,000 of retained profit as a cash buffer against the problems in the case, namely off-cut waste costing $16 per kilogram and a defect rate that has risen to 3.6%. With fixed costs of $175,000 a year and car production growing only 3.2%, holding that reserve protects the 7-day delivery lead time and avoids a cash crisis if a batch of gaskets has to be remade.

Point 2: Borrowing the $180,000 spreads the cost of the $480,000 machine over time instead of draining the partnership's own funds at once, preserving working capital for raw rubber and wages. It also leaves the partners' personal capital untouched, so the business can fund the 12 staff requiring injection-moulding certification from revenue rather than asking the partners for more money. Used alongside the $300,000 retained profit, the loan keeps the 45,000-unit operation liquid while it adjusts to the new machine.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified, max 2.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to TRM's waste, costs, liquidity and ownership.

questions.question_text: TRM is promoting its new recycled-rubber seals. Consider sponsorship of a motorsport team, advertising in automotive supplier magazines, or listings on industrial e-commerce marketplaces. Which should TRM choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Motorsport sponsorship: Associating TRM with a racing team would raise brand recognition quickly among car enthusiasts and could suggest high-performance rubber, but it is extremely expensive for a 38-staff partnership and reaches the general public rather than the procurement engineers who buy 45,000 gaskets. With fixed costs of $175,000 and a $180,000 loan, such spend would be hard to justify against the 3.6% defect problem.

Automotive supplier magazines: Print advertisements would reach a specialist readership and could explain the recycled-rubber feed message, which 71% of 200 surveyed buyers prefer. However, magazines have long lead times, high costs and no immediate response mechanism, and only 48% of buyers check environmental credentials, so much of the spend would not convert into orders for a small firm with a 7-day lead time.

Industrial e-commerce listings: Listing the seals on established B2B marketplaces puts TRM in front of buyers actively searching for gaskets, is relatively low-cost and gives measurable enquiries and orders. The recycled-rubber story can be shown in the product description, appealing directly to the 71% who prefer such suppliers. Listings alone do not build deep brand loyalty and depend on good product data and prompt fulfilment, but they suit a small partnership.

Recommendation: TRM should choose industrial e-commerce listings, supported by modest magazine advertising later. Marketplaces reach active buyers cheaply and measurably, which matters against $175,000 fixed costs and a $180,000 loan. Motorsport sponsorship is rejected as unaffordable and aimed at the wrong audience, and magazine advertising alone is rejected as slow and hard to measure; online listings can generate the volume that makes later print worthwhile.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited description of the three promotional options with minimal application to TRM.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of at least two options with advantages and disadvantages in the context of TRM and some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three options applied to TRM with a justified recommendation explaining why motorsport sponsorship and magazine-only advertising are rejected.

questions.question_text: TRM's labour turnover has reached 14%. Explain two benefits for TRM of its flat structure with laissez-faire leadership in motivating its production team.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A flat structure with laissez-faire leadership gives TRM's 38 experienced moulding operators real autonomy over how they set up their machines and solve problems, which can satisfy esteem needs and raise job satisfaction. In a small partnership there are few layers, so skilled staff are trusted rather than closely supervised; that freedom can reduce the 14% labour turnover by making operators want to stay, avoiding repeated recruitment and the $780-per-employee cost of replacing certified staff.

Point 2: Delegating decisions speeds problem-solving on the factory floor, which matters with off-cut waste costing $16 per kilogram and a defect rate that has risen from 2.4% to 3.6%. Operators who can adjust a mould immediately prevent waste and keep the 7-day delivery lead time, supporting the 71% of 200 surveyed buyers who prefer recycled-rubber suppliers. Dev Tarrant can then focus on the $480,000 investment and the 45,000-unit target instead of approving routine choices, while the 12 staff needing certification can learn by doing.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified, max 2.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation linked to TRM's turnover, waste, delivery and structure.

questions.question_text: TRM must upskill 12 staff to operate the new injection-moulding machine. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job courses at the local college. Which should TRM choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training beside the moulding machine is tailored to TRM's own equipment, costs no fees and keeps all 12 staff producing gaskets while they learn, protecting the 11,250 units made each quarter and the 7-day delivery lead time. It also lets experienced partners coach workers on reducing the 3.6% defect rate and the $16-per-kilogram off-cut waste. Its limitations are that trainers' own output falls, that informal habits may be copied, and that no certificate is issued even though the audit found 12 of 38 staff lack injection-moulding certification.

Off-the-job courses: The local college course at $780 per employee gives structured skills and a recognised qualification for all 12 staff, costing $9,360 in total, affordable beside the $480,000 machine. Formal certification supports the 71% of 200 surveyed buyers who prefer recycled-rubber suppliers and helps cut waste through better machine settings. However, it takes 12 of a workforce of 38 away from production, risking the 45,000-unit target and the 7-day lead time, and the generic content may need site-specific follow-up. With labour turnover at 14%, newly qualified staff could also leave.

Decision: TRM should choose on-the-job training, with short college modules for the most senior operators. It is cheap, machine-specific and protects output and delivery while the partnership absorbs a $180,000 loan. Full off-the-job training is rejected because removing 12 of 38 staff would disrupt the 7-day lead time and the 45,000-unit target, and the $9,360 fee can be spent later once the machine is stable and the 3.6% defect rate is understood.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to TRM.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of TRM.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods applied to TRM with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and certification.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how TRM's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 25,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $7.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 20,000 units vs 45,000 output; pricing/discount modelling against $175,000 fixed costs; loan-service volume for the $480,000 machine; and unit-cost benchmarking at $12.89 to reduce 3.6% defects and off-cut waste.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $175,000 ÷ ($16.00 − $9.00) = $175,000 ÷ $7.00 = 25,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 25,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $16.00 − $9.00 = $7.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $7.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways TRM's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. The partners can compare the 25,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 45,000 units, a margin of safety of 20,000 units, to judge whether the new $480,000 machine can be afforded from the $180,000 loan and $300,000 retained profit.
2. Contribution per unit of $7.00 lets TRM test pricing with buyers: a 5% price cut to $15.20 would leave $6.20 contribution, still covering the $175,000 fixed costs at current volume, so managers can judge discount requests from car manufacturers.
3. Fixed costs of $175,000 and contribution of $7.00 set the volume needed to service the loan and show how much of the 3.2% growth in car production TRM must capture to stay safe.
4. Average total cost ($175,000 ÷ 45,000 units + $9.00 = $12.89 a unit) gives a benchmark for the 3.6% defect rate and $16-per-kilogram off-cut waste, and a basis for pressing suppliers over the 8.7% rise in rubber input costs.

working_marks: 1 mark for the correct formula/method and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii), max 4.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TRM's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has TRM's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.59 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.81 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 1.02 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.10 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $95,000 inventories + $130,000 trade receivables + $38,000 cash = $263,000; 2025 current assets = $110,000 + $118,000 + $52,000 = $280,000. Short-term cover for 2024 is $263,000 ÷ $165,000 = 1.59 and for 2025 is $280,000 ÷ $155,000 = 1.81. Excluding inventories, ($263,000 − $95,000) ÷ $165,000 = 1.02 in 2024 and ($280,000 − $110,000) ÷ $155,000 = 1.10 in 2025.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved clearly. Current assets rose from $263,000 to $280,000 while current liabilities fell from $165,000 to $155,000, lifting short-term cover from 1.59 to 1.81. The acid test also rose from 1.02 to 1.10, so TRM is less dependent on selling inventory to meet debts, which helps while it services a $180,000 loan and buys the $480,000 machine. Receivables fell from $130,000 to $118,000, freeing cash, although inventories grew from $95,000 to $110,000, and with a 3.6% defect rate some stock may prove slow to sell. The partnership has also moved cash from $38,000 to $52,000 while funding the $480,000 machine, so it has kept a usable buffer for the 7-day delivery promise and the $180,000 loan.

Conclusion: TRM's financial position has improved. Both measures are higher and the improvement does not rest on inventory alone, since the acid-test rise confirms it. Management should keep control of the rising stock and the 14% labour turnover, but the balance sheet can support the expansion.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates both ratios for 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether TRM's position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TRM of fitting the recycled-rubber feed system to its new moulding machine.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: A recycled-rubber feed system would let TRM reuse off-cuts that currently cost $16 per kilogram in waste, cutting the $9.00 variable cost per unit and helping counter the 8.7% rise in rubber input costs. It also matches the 71% of 200 surveyed automotive buyers who prefer suppliers using recycled rubber and the 48% who check environmental credentials, supporting sales of the 45,000 units and the 7-day delivery promise at the $16.00 selling price.

Disadvantage: The feed system adds cost to the $480,000 machine on top of a $180,000 loan and fixed costs of $175,000 a year, so it raises break-even risk if car production grows only 3.2%. Recycled feed may also vary in quality, which could worsen the defect rate of 3.6% (already up from 2.4%) and the 27 monthly complaints, and with labour turnover at 14% and 12 of 38 staff uncertified, operators may need extra training to run the system consistently.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to TRM's waste, survey and investment.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 4.50%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase and the 8.7% rise in rubber input costs will affect TRM. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.50%): If TRM's $180,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the extra interest is 0.75% of $180,000 = $1,350 a year (0.0075 × $180,000), small against fixed costs of $175,000, and nil if the loan is fixed. The more meaningful effect is that dearer credit discourages car buyers, whose production is forecast to grow only 3.2%, so TRM may struggle to sell all 45,000 units. Fixing the rate would remove most of this risk.

Minimum wage increase (7.1%, to $14.46 per hour): With a workforce of 38, many moulding and packing jobs are hourly paid, so the wage bill rises and cannot be avoided. The insert states no hours worked or individual pay, so an annual total would be invented; the defensible comparison is productivity of 45,000 units ÷ 38 staff = 1,184 units per worker. If productivity holds, the $7.00 contribution can absorb the rise; if labour turnover of 14% persists, retraining costs and lower output will squeeze the $12.89 average total cost.

Input cost inflation (8.7% rubber): The $9.00 variable cost includes rubber, but the insert does not decompose it, so only a bound is honest: if the whole variable cost rose 8.7% that adds 8.7% × $9.00 = $0.78 per unit, about $35,000 a year at 45,000 units (45,000 × $0.78). The recycled-rubber feed system can offset some of this, but not all of a broad input-price rise.

Conclusion: The 8.7% rise in rubber input costs will have the greatest impact. It applies to every one of the 45,000 units and directly reduces the $7.00 contribution that must cover $175,000 fixed costs and the $180,000 loan. The interest rise is tiny and fixable, and the wage rise can be managed through productivity and retention; input inflation is the threat TRM can least control.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to TRM.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on TRM's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes applied to TRM with a well-justified judgement that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
